lede: Logs and event feeds usually arrive as JSON Lines: one JSON record per line. Most lines are fine; the few that aren't decide whether your job crashes, silently loses data, or tells you what went wrong.
objectives: Read JSON Lines with `spark.read.json`, with and without a schema
Read a file that holds one JSON array with `multiLine=True`
Drop or keep malformed records with `mode` and `columnNameOfCorruptRecord`
Tell a broken line from a record with a missing field or a value of the wrong type

blocks.md: `application_logs_raw` is an application log file before parsing, one line per row in a `value` column. Each good line is one JSON record. A few lines aren't: the shipper cut one record off halfway and then resent it whole, another record lost its closing `}`, and one line is a plain-text traceback.

blocks.title: The log file as text
blocks.note: Thirteen lines for ten log records. Look at lines 4, 8 and 12: the first two start like JSON but don't finish properly, and the third isn't JSON at all.

blocks.md:
As in the CSV lesson, each example first saves the text as a file, here `/tmp/logs/app`, and reads it back.

`spark.read.json(path)` reads **JSON Lines**: it expects one complete record on each line. Without a schema it reads the data once to work out the columns and their types, and puts any line it can't parse into an extra column, `_corrupt_record`.

blocks.title: Let Spark work out the schema
blocks.note: Every field became text, including `logged_at`, and `attributes` became a struct with every key seen in any line. The three broken lines have NULL in every field and their raw text in `_corrupt_record`. LOG-000004 and LOG-000007 also appear as good records, from the copies that arrived whole.

blocks.md:
A schema fixes the types and skips the extra pass. The options for bad records are the ones you know from CSV:

- `PERMISSIVE` (the default) keeps a bad line as a row of NULLs. Add a text column to the schema and name it in `columnNameOfCorruptRecord` to keep the raw line.
- `DROPMALFORMED` leaves bad lines out.
- `FAILFAST` stops the job at the first one.

Fields that aren't in the schema are simply not read, so you can take only the part of each record you need.

blocks.title: Keep or drop the bad lines
blocks.code:
application_logs_raw.write.mode("overwrite").text("/tmp/logs/app")

schema = "log_id STRING, logged_at TIMESTAMP, level STRING, service STRING, message STRING"

flagged = spark.read.json("/tmp/logs/app", schema=schema + ", bad_record STRING", columnNameOfCorruptRecord="bad_record")
flagged.select("log_id", "level", "bad_record").show(truncate=50)

clean = spark.read.json("/tmp/logs/app", schema=schema, mode="DROPMALFORMED")
clean.show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: `flagged` has all thirteen lines; the three bad ones have no `log_id` and keep their text in `bad_record`. `clean` has exactly the ten log records, with `logged_at` as a real timestamp.

blocks.md:
Not every problem is a broken line. A record can be valid JSON and still not fit the schema:

- A **missing field** is just NULL. The record isn't malformed.
- A value of the **wrong type**, such as text that isn't a number for an `INT` field, makes the record malformed. In `PERMISSIVE` mode the other fields are still read, the bad one is NULL, and the raw line is kept.
- A blank line is skipped.

blocks.title: Missing fields and wrong types
blocks.code:
lines = [
    '{"log_id": "T1", "level": "INFO", "latency_ms": 42}',
    '{"log_id": "T2", "level": "WARN"}',
    '{"log_id": "T3", "level": "INFO", "latency_ms": "slow"}',
    '',
    '{"log_id": "T4", "level": "ERROR", "latency_ms": 1240}',
]
with open("/tmp/logs_types.jsonl", "w") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")

schema = "log_id STRING, level STRING, latency_ms INT, bad_record STRING"
spark.read.json("/tmp/logs_types.jsonl", schema=schema, columnNameOfCorruptRecord="bad_record").show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: T2 has no `latency_ms`, so it's NULL and the record is fine. T3's `"slow"` isn't an `INT`: the record is flagged, but its `log_id` and `level` were still read. The blank line gives no row. This small file is written with plain Python, which can write to `/tmp` too.

blocks.md: Some systems write one big JSON **array** instead of one record per line, often spread over many lines. Read line by line, every line is a fragment. `multiLine=True` tells Spark to parse each file as a whole JSON document; an array becomes one row per element.

blocks.title: One JSON array across many lines
blocks.code:
with open("/tmp/logs_array.json", "w") as f:
    f.write('[\n  {"log_id": "A1", "level": "INFO"},\n  {"log_id": "A2", "level": "WARN"}\n]\n')

spark.read.json("/tmp/logs_array.json").show()
spark.read.json("/tmp/logs_array.json", multiLine=True).show()
blocks.note: Line by line, `[` and `]` are bad records and each element happens to fit on its own line. With `multiLine=True` the whole file is one array, and its two elements become two clean rows.

blocks.title: Asking only for the bad records
blocks.code:
application_logs_raw.write.mode("overwrite").text("/tmp/logs/app")

schema = "log_id STRING, logged_at TIMESTAMP, level STRING, service STRING, message STRING, bad_record STRING"
logs = spark.read.json("/tmp/logs/app", schema=schema, columnNameOfCorruptRecord="bad_record")
logs.select("bad_record").show()
blocks.note: Spark refuses a query on a raw JSON or CSV file that reads only the corrupt-record column, because with no other field asked for it can't reliably tell which lines are bad. Select another column with it, such as `log_id`, as the earlier example does.

concept.prompt: A file holds one JSON array of records, spread over many lines. How do you read it?
concept.why: By default `spark.read.json` expects one record per line. `multiLine=True` parses each file as one JSON document, and an array gives one row per element.

concept.prompt: In `PERMISSIVE` mode with a schema, a record has `"latency_ms": "slow"` for an `INT` field. What happens?
choices: The record is kept, `latency_ms` is NULL, its other fields are read, and the raw line goes to the corrupt-record column
concept.why: A wrong type makes the record malformed. `PERMISSIVE` keeps it, reads what it can, and puts the raw line in the column named by `columnNameOfCorruptRecord`.

concept.prompt: A record has no `trace_id` field, but the schema has one. Is it malformed?
choices: No, but the whole row is NULL
concept.why: A missing field is read as NULL. Only lines that aren't valid JSON, or values of the wrong type, are malformed.

review: `spark.read.json(path)` reads JSON Lines: one record per line. Without a schema it scans the data to guess types and adds `_corrupt_record` for lines it can't parse.
A schema sets the types, skips the extra scan, and reads only the fields you list.
`mode` works as for CSV: `PERMISSIVE` keeps bad lines, `DROPMALFORMED` drops them, `FAILFAST` stops. `columnNameOfCorruptRecord` keeps the raw text.
A missing field is NULL, not malformed. A value of the wrong type makes the record malformed, but `PERMISSIVE` still reads its other fields.
`multiLine=True` reads each file as one JSON document, such as an array spread over many lines.
A query on a raw file can't read only the corrupt-record column; select another column with it.
